title: MB1-03016
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimant), a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is claiming that he is a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) because of his alleged imputed political opinion given that he is a member of the UDPS.

The claimant also states that he is "a person in need of protection" because he is afraid of being arrested, detained and tortured by the government of Joseph Kabila and the Agence Nationale de Renseignements (ANR) [national intelligence agency] because he is a member of the opposition and he participated in a few demonstrations.

The claimant essentially alleged the following facts. He had a permanent job as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) from XXXX 2005 until he left the DRC in XXXX 2011. The claimant stated that he had problems because of his activism as a member of the UDPS, which he had been a member of since 1994. He had problems because of his political affiliations, among other things, in 2006, 2010 and 2011. The claimant stated that, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010 (amended to XXXX), he participated in a march organized by the various opposition parties demanding that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant was arrested along with XXXX other people. He was beaten during transportation to prison. When he was released from prison (amended to upon his arrival in prison) the authorities took his photograph. The claimant was released from prison without being questioned two days later. On XXXX XXXX, 2011, masked men went to his house at 4:00 a.m., but luckily, he escaped out the window. His wife was gang raped. The attackers stole everything of value that he possessed. On XXXX XXXX, 2011, at his sister's (amended to at his cousin's) home, a friend of his brother's who works for the XXXX gave him the photograph that had been taken when he was released (amended to arrested). In XXXX 2011, his employer recommended that he take a course in Canada. Through his NGO contacts, the claimant obtained a false letter from a senior XXXX XXXX official in the DRC that stated that he was an employee sent to take a course in Montréal. A Canadian visitor's visa was issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. He spent two weeks taking the course he was registered for in Montréal.
The claimant went to the CIC office on May 19, 2011, XXXX weeks after his arrival, to claim refugee protection.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons. ANALYSIS Identity

To establish his identity, the claimant submitted a copy of his passport from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the original of which was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC).1
The panel finds that this is an acceptable identity document under section 106 of the IRPA. Credibility

The claimant failed to credibly establish the material facts alleged in support of his claim for refugee protection, namely that he left the DRC because of the facts alleged in his account. The claimant is not a trustworthy witness. He lied to the panel, deliberately concealed facts and tried to mislead the panel by submitting false documents. The claimant left his country legally even though he claimed to be wanted by the ANR.
The claimant is not a credible witness. He did not establish that he participated in a march in XXXX or XXXX 2010 or that he was arrested.

The claimant stated that he is a member of UDPS. He submitted a UDPS card (C-4) dated 1994. The claimant established that he is a member of the party. The claimant submitted a letter dated March 25, 2013 (C-7), which states that he is regularly a registered member. He then explained in very general terms that he fled the Democratic Republic of the Congo to escape the abuses of the existing dictatorial power and that he is seeking safe haven.

In his testimony, the claimant stated that he came to Canada to take a course at his employer's request. He spent two weeks taking the course in Montréal. He stated that he planned to return to the DRC, which is the reason he gave for not claiming refugee protection at the airport or within a few days of arriving. Nowhere in the letter does UPDS management mention that the claimant was detained or wanted by the ANR. The letter simply establishes that the claimant was a registered member of UDPS.

The claimant submitted four lists of amendments to his PIF and his narrative: June 15, 2011; May 16, 2013; July 8, 2013; and October 13, 2013. These amendments are significant, but no credible or reasonable explanation justifies them. The claimant made the following amendments: he added a family member to question 4. He amended the fact that the ANR officer, a friend of the family, went to see him at his sister's (amended to his cousin's). How could the claimant have mixed up his sister and his cousin when the encounter was supposed to have taken place a few days before his departure for Canada?

The claimant stated that he had participated in a big demonstration to protest XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX of 2010. In an amendment on June 15, 2011, the claimant changed the month of the demonstration he claimed to have attended in XXXX 2010 to XXXX and also changed the period of his detention. The claimant provided no valid explanation for why he did not remember the month in which he was allegedly arrested and detained.

The claimant amended his PIF when the panel discovered, upon receiving confirmation of the fingerprints from the American authorities (produced in Exhibit A-3), that the claimant had applied for a visa for the United States three times: in 2005, 2008 and XXXX 2010. The claimant admitted to the panel that he had lied on his PIF by not declaring these facts because he did not want to jeopardize his claim for refugee protection and he apologized. It is not so much the fact that the claimant applied for an American visa three times that jeopardizes his claim for refugee protection; it is the fact that the claimant is not a witness the panel can trust.

The claimant also amended his Personal Information Form (PIF) to state that his photograph was taken when he was arrested in XXXX 2010 to state that the photograph was taken when he was released. Once again, it is reasonable to believe that the claimant would remember whether the photograph had been taken when he was arrested or when he was released. All these amendments to his narrative undermine his credibility and raise serious doubts about whether the claimant experienced the alleged facts.

According to the case law, the panel is entitled to draw a negative inference concerning credibility because of a major amendment or addition to the PIF.2 In this case, the amendments are significant.

The panel knows why the claimant amended the allegation about when the photograph was taken because, according to his narrative, he was arrested by guards who were not in uniform (line 58 and below of the narrative). However, in the photograph submitted as evidence under C-7, the soldiers are in uniform. The photograph has nothing to do with an arrest. It is a group photograph, and the people in it are posing for the photograph. If the authorities had wanted to photograph the claimant as a suspect and member of the opposition, they would have taken a [translation] "mug shot" of the claimant, that is, a close-up. It is clear that the claimant attempted to mislead the panel by submitting this photograph, which was taken under other circumstances. The claimant stated that he got the photograph from an ANR officer who gave it to him at his sister's (amended to his cousin's) home. Submitting this false photograph as evidence destroys his credibility because, even though the claimant apologized for lying, he continued trying to mislead the panel.

When questioned by the panel about why he was listed in the visa application (in evidence as A-4) as being the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX when he was really a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the claimant explained that he was able to get a false XXXX letter from a colleague from another NGO in the DRC so that he could be sure of getting into Canada. The claimant did not mention this fact in his narrative but stated that he had come to participate in volunteer training for his employer. It is therefore reasonable to believe that the claimant had access to this type of service (self-ving document) through his NGO colleagues since he himself had worked in the field for over 10 years. The claimant's lack of transparency in disclosing these facts-he did so only when he had no other choice-undermines his credibility.
The claimant tried to mislead the panel by submitting false documents, which destroys his credibility.

Justice Martineau states that if a claimant submits false documents to support a claim for refugee protection, it has consequences with respect to the claimant's credibility:3 [7] Producing a false document to support allegations in a refugee claim must not be minimized by the Court and legitimately allows the tribunal to doubt a claimant's credibility. (Rahaman v. Canada, 2007 FC 108, paragraphs 15 to 17).

The claimant is not a credible witness. He told an implausible story about how masked officers tried to arrest him in XXXX 2011. His wife allegedly answered the door because she thought that bakers were coming to deliver bread at 4:00 a.m. for their children. Even though the house was besieged by armed masked men who had come to arrest the claimant, he alleged that he was able to jump out the window because the soldiers or ANR officers had not thought to surround the house. The panel was able to watch the claimant while he related these facts, and it is clear that he was lying and did not actually experience the events he was relating. The panel gives no probative value to the letter from his wife produced in C-6 or to the lawyer who claimed to be aware of the claimant's problems, and that is because of his general lack of credibility.

In Ren,4 Justice Mainville stated that the Canadian system is based on the candour of the refugee protection claimants and that it is reasonable that misleading the panel would have consequences on the claimant's credibility, particularly if the claimant continues to do so, as is the case, even after apologizing. The judge states: [15] The Applicant takes issue with the finding of the Panel that his credibility was tainted by the fact he lied to Canadian immigration officials by not disclosing that he had resided in the United States of America from April 2001 to January 2005, had pursued unsuccessfully a refugee claim there and had subsequently returned to China. The Applicant says this adverse credibility finding is not reasonable since the Panel failed to accept his contrition about this lack of truthfulness. The Applicant argues that he is a simple and uneducated man and that he unwisely relied on the advice of the "snakehead" who brought him to Canada and who told him not to reveal this information. He now asks the Canadian authorities to forgive him. [16] I find no merit to this argument. Refugee determinations in Canada are based on voluntary and truthful declarations from claimants. The Applicant decided not to reveal key information to Canadian authorities since he believed this would facilitate his access to Canada. His failures to declare his stay in the USA, his unsuccessful refugee claim there and his eventual return to China in 2005 clearly affect his credibility, and it was entirely reasonable for the Panel to draw an adverse inference from this.

The panel could also talk about how the claimant did not claim refugee protection upon arriving in Canada but waited three weeks to do so. Instead, he attended volunteer training. The claimant testified that he had intended to return to the DRC after the training despite the fact that, according to his alleged and not very credible narrative, his wife had just been gang raped because of him. He also left with his passport and a Canadian visa even though he claimed to be wanted by the ANR, which is another valid reason to doubt his credibility.

In Balwant Singh,5 Justice Shore states that the fact that the claimant used his own passport to leave India undermined the claimant's credibility when he alleged that he was a wanted person and feared the authorities. The judge states: [10] The RPD reasonably concluded that the fact that Mr. Balwant Singh used his own passport to leave India demonstrated that he did not fear the central authorities. (Choque v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1997), 73 A.C.W.S. (3d) 308, [1997] F.C.J. No. 1017 (QL); Ccanto v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) 1994, 73 F.T.R. 144, 46 A.C.W.S. (3d) 309; Singh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 958, [2009] F.C.J. No. 1169 (QL)).
The claimant did not credibly establish that he is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA.

The claimant was not credible and had no other evidence to support his claim of being a "person in need of protection," so the panel will not undertake a separate analysis of section 97 of the IRPA.6 CONCLUSION

Having considered all the evidence, the panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to his country.

For all these reasons, XXXX XXXX XXXX claim for refugee protection is rejected.
